lead: The Apostles' Fast begins today, and the readings set the apostles before us. In the Gospel Jesus gives the Twelve authority and Matthew records their names, from “first, Simon, also known as Peter” to Judas Iscariot. Paul tells the Corinthians how to think of those who serve the Church: “as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries”, of whom one thing is required, that they be found trustworthy. The key words are authority and faithfulness.

set: The church at Corinth was divided into parties: “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” “I belong to Cephas” (1:12). In chapter 3 Paul answers that he and Apollos are only servants: one planted, the other watered, but God gave the growth (3:6). Chapter 4 opens with the conclusion: this is how you should regard us. Some at Corinth were also judging Paul and comparing him unfavourably with others; he answers that only the Lord can judge.
str: v. 1: servants of Christ, stewards of God's mysteries.
v. 2: what is required of stewards: trustworthiness.
vv. 3–4: Paul is not troubled by human judgment, nor does he judge himself; the Lord judges.
v. 5: wait for the Lord, who will bring hidden things to light.
kw: A helper who carries out another's orders. Luke uses the same word for John Mark, who assisted Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:5). The minister is never the owner of the work.
The manager of a household, often a trusted slave, who looked after the master's goods and gave each member of the household what was needed. He owned nothing; he answered for everything.
In Paul, God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Christ (2:7). The Eastern Churches came to call the sacraments the Holy Mysteries, in Syriac rāzē, because in them that plan is given to us.
vv: Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries.
Two images: servants who obey, stewards who distribute. The ministers of the Church do not invent the faith or the sacraments; they hand on what they have received (11:23).
Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.
Not brilliance, not popularity, but faithfulness. The same is asked of every Christian who has been given something to care for: a family, a gift, a task in the parish.
It is the Lord who judges me.
Paul's conscience is clear, but he knows that a clear conscience is not the final verdict. Only God sees the whole heart.
Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes,
This is not a ban on all judgment of right and wrong; Paul himself gives firm judgments in chapter 5. It forbids judging the hidden motives of others, which only the Lord can bring to light.
ch: The Catechism explains that the Greek word mystērion was rendered in Latin by two words, mysterium and sacramentum, so that the sacraments are the signs and instruments by which the one mystery of Christ is given to us (CCC 774). The Church has always applied this verse to bishops and priests, who are stewards of the Holy Mysteries, and it reminds them that faithfulness is what the Lord asks. It reminds the faithful, too, that they should pray for their pastors more than they judge them.

r.h: The names of the twelve apostles
set: Just before this passage Jesus sees the crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” and tells his disciples to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers (9:36–38). Now he himself sends labourers. Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses in his Gospel, the missionary discourse, and it begins by naming those who are sent.
str: v. 1: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and every disease.
vv. 2–4: the names of the twelve apostles, in pairs.
kw: Not their own power but a share in the authority of Jesus himself, who has shown it over sickness, sin and the demons (chapters 8–9).
This is the only place where Matthew uses the word. An apostle is a messenger who carries the authority of the one who sends him.

Peter stands first in every list of the apostles in the New Testament, and Judas Iscariot is last in every Gospel list. Matthew adds the word “first”, which is not needed for counting; it marks Peter's place.
vv: Then Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease and every sickness.
The words “every disease and every sickness” repeat what Matthew has said of Jesus himself (4:23; 9:35). The apostles are sent to do what Jesus does.
These are the names of the twelve apostles: first, Simon, also known as Peter,
Twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus is gathering the people of God anew, and the Twelve are its foundation (Revelation 21:14).
Thomas and Matthew the tax collector;

Only Matthew's list adds “the tax collector” to his own name, remembering where the Lord found him (9:9). Thomas, named beside him, is the apostle whom the Christians of India have honoured as their father in faith.
Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed him.

“Cananaean” is not about Canaan; it comes from an Aramaic word meaning “zealous”, and Luke calls him “the Zealot” (Luke 6:15). The list ends soberly with Judas: to be chosen is a gift that must be kept by faithfulness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Lord Jesus gave his community a structure that will remain until the kingdom is fully achieved: he chose the Twelve with Peter as their head, and they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765). It also teaches that Simon Peter holds the first place in the college of the Twelve (CCC 552). The bishops are the successors of the apostles, and through them the authority given in today's Gospel continues in the Church.

qa: Why does the Church fast so soon after Pentecost?

Jesus said that his disciples would fast when the bridegroom was taken away from them (Matthew 9:15). After the Ascension and Pentecost the Church sets out on her mission, and in Acts the first Christians fast before sending out missionaries: “while they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul’” (Acts 13:2–3). St Leo the Great preached in Rome on a fast after Pentecost and spoke of it as handed down from the apostles (Sermons on the Pentecost fast, in substance). The Apostles' Fast is a fast for mission, kept in the company of the apostles.
rite: Today the Apostles' Fast, the Shleeha Nombu, begins in our Church, and it is kept until the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The fast is not only a discipline of food. It is a time to pray for the Church's mission and for those who carry it: the Holy Father, our bishops and priests, missionaries and catechists. Today's Gospel gives the fast its faces, the twelve names. It is good to pray for one apostle each day, and to remember especially St Thomas, through whose preaching, as our tradition holds, the faith first came to our land.
study: Paul says that stewards must be found trustworthy. What has God entrusted to me, and am I faithful in caring for it?
How will I keep the Apostles' Fast this year: what will I give up, and for whose mission will I pray?
